tasks.task_description: Goal: build an optimal 5-year, $100M/yr investment strategy for the Goodgrant Foundation that (a) produces a 1-to-N optimized and prioritized candidate list of schools, (b) assigns an investment amount per school, (c) estimates the return on investment in a form appropriate for a charitable education funder, and (d) specifies the time duration over which funds should be provided, maximizing the likelihood of a strong positive effect on student performance without duplicating the focus of other large grantmakers. Scope: ~3,000 candidate U.S. post-secondary institutions (IPEDS UID list) joined to the College Scorecard 'Most Recent Cohorts' data; the model must be based on a meaningful, defensible subset of these data. This container addresses the full task as one integrated subtask: data cleaning, ROI definition, school scoring, portfolio construction, and the resulting prioritized list with per-school amounts.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions. (1) The funded activity is a student-success program (tutoring, advising, case management) because that is what a restricted educational-performance grant is spent on first in practice; the expert confirmed grant dollars go first to direct incremental costs of the goal — personnel (50-70% of a program grant), then student financial support if the goal is access/retention, then program operations, then 10-20% indirect overhead (exchange 1). (2) A lump-sum grant can only change outcomes if the school can deploy it into net-new direct program cost; the binding limits are restricted-purpose terms, absorptive (management) capacity, the recurring-cost/salary cliff at year 5, scale mismatch (a grant far larger than the institution's scale cannot be spent productively), and board/accreditation scrutiny (exchange 2). (3) Effects are time-lagged: retention effects are visible within 1-2 semesters; graduation effects take 3-5 years (year ~4 for 4-year cohorts, years 2-3 for 2-year/150%-time cohorts) and are modest, a few percentage points (exchange 3). (4) Post-grant persistence is two-branch: if the program is discontinued, the gain decays to baseline within ~2-4 years leaving a ~0-1 pp residual; if the college absorbs the recurring cost, roughly half or more persists (exchange 4). (5) Colleges that keep programs after the grant ends are those with surpluses/healthy endowments, public institutions with a state funding path, programs proven on their own metrics, activities embedded in existing structures, and larger institutions with small marginal cost per student; small tuition-dependent, thin-margin, enrollment-pressured colleges — precisely the typical grant target — usually do not (exchange 5). (6) Per-student program cost is $100-300 (light-touch), $500-1,500 (structured, staff-intensive), $2,000-5,000+ (high-intensity); we use $1,000/student/yr (interval [500,1500]) as the mid-intensity design a foundation would expect (exchange 6). (7) Program effect size: targeted advising/tutoring yields ~2-5 pp graduation gain (up to ~10 pp for intensive, well-implemented programs for disadvantaged students); structured advising 3-8 pp; tutoring alone 1-3 pp; effects shrink with scale and lower intensity (exchange 7). (8) Allocation style: a middle path — a modest number of larger concentrated grants to the strongest candidates plus smaller awards to a wider set — because pure breadth produces undetectable effects and pure concentration over-concentrates risk; concentration also lowers admin cost per dollar (exchange 8). (9) Portfolio size: a foundation staff can keep close tabs on ~20-50 grantees (deep engagement ~10-25 per program officer), so the funded portfolio is ~40-46 schools (exchange 9). (10) The outcome a foundation trusts most to judge a grant is the near-term, program-linked, independently verifiable measure — retention/persistence and credit accumulation — with graduation treated as long-run confirmation, not proof (exchange 10). Modeling approach and why it is sound: a deterministic, transparent scoring-and-allocation model rather than a black box, because the deliverable is a defensible recommendation to a CFO. The mechanism chain from exchanges 1-5 (spend -> direct program cost -> students served -> near-term retention gain -> lagged completion gain -> post-grant persistence) is encoded as a small set of equations with all empirical parameters calibrated to the exchanges; the Scorecard supplies the per-school state (retention, completion, enrollment, Pell share, control, degree mix) that the equations act on. The approach is sound because every structural choice is grounded in stated practice, every number is either in the dataset or in the calibrated parameter table below, and the allocation respects the operational constraints (scale cap, detectability floor, engagement capacity) rather than assuming unbounded effectiveness.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: DATA SUBSET AND CLEANING. From the 2,977 candidate UNITIDs (no duplicates) we join to the 7,804-row Scorecard cohort file on UNITID: 2,935 match (42 candidates lack any Scorecard row and are dropped). Numeric fields are coerced with 'PrivacySuppressed' and non-numeric tokens -> NaN; affected counts: C150_4_POOLED_SUPP 51 suppressed, C200_L4_POOLED_SUPP 10, GRAD_DEBT_MDN10YR_SUPP 247, RPY_3YR_RT_SUPP 93, md_earn_wne_p10 120, gt_25k_p6 126. A school is eligible if it has at least one of RET_FT4 (4-yr retention) or C150_4_POOLED_SUPP (6-yr completion): 2,901 eligible (2,746 have both). We keep UGDS between 500 and 20,000 (the practical band for a multi-student program). The 2015 Scorecard has no balance sheet, endowment, or surplus field, so fiscal headroom is proxied (documented limitation). VARIABLES USED. UGDS = undergraduate enrollment; PCTPELL = share receiving Pell (need proxy); RET_FT4 / RET_FTL4 = first-time full-time retention at 4-yr / <4-yr institutions (retention outcome); C150_4_POOLED_SUPP / C200_L4_POOLED_SUPP = 150% (6-yr) / 200% (4-yr) pooled completion (completion outcome); CONTROL (1=public) and NPT41_PUB/NPT42_PRIV (net price by income/control) for the fiscal proxy; PCIP11/14/15/51/52/13/44/45/26/27/40 (CS, engineering, engineering tech, health, business, education, public admin/social service, bio, math, physical sciences) summed into mix_high as a program-capability proxy; is_lt4 = less-than-four-year flag (RET_FTL4 present / C200 present). PER-SCHOOL MODEL. For a grant G to school i: (a) scale-mismatch cap: G_i = min(G_i, K_SCALE * 5 * C_PROG * UGDS_i) — a grant cannot exceed a fraction K_SCALE of the 5-year program capacity, encoding that a grant far larger than the institution's scale cannot be spent productively (exchange 2). (b) students funded: funded_i = min(G_i / (5*C_PROG), UGDS_i); served share s_i = funded_i/UGDS_i. (c) completion gain (pp): delta_i = clip(DELTA0 * (0.5 + 0.5*s_i) * (1 + 0.5*PCTPELL_i), DELTA_MIN, DELTA_MAX) — base gain DELTA0, rising with intensity (served share) and need (Pell), capped at the intensive-program ceiling (exchange 7). (d) retention gain (pp): ret_gain_i = clip(1.2*delta_i, 0.5, 8). (e) timing within the 5-year window (years 1-5): completion ramp R_t = clip((t-1)/(T_ramp-1),0,1) with T_ramp = 4 for 4-yr, 3 for 2-yr schools (exchange 3); retention ramp Rret_t = 0.5*clip(t/2,0,1) + 0.5*R_t (visible in 1-2 semesters). in_win_i = W_RET*mean_t(Rret_t)*ret_gain_i + W_COMP*mean_t(R_t)*delta_i — the composite outcome realizable inside the window, weighted W_RET=0.6 / W_COMP=0.4 toward the trusted near-term retention measure (exchange 10). (f) post-window tail: tail_i = in_win_i * (p_persist_i / 0.5) * 0.5, where p_persist_i = q_i*P_ABSORB + (1-q_i)*P_FADE is the expected share of the gain that survives the year-5 cliff (exchange 4), half-weighted as in-progress cohorts converting in years 6-9. total_pp_i = in_win_i + tail_i. (g) absorption probability (exchange 5): q_i = clip(0.25*(CONTROL_i==1) + 0.35*clip((ln UGDS_i - ln 800)/(ln 8000 - ln 800),0,1) + 0.40*(0.6*(CONTROL_i==1) + 0.4*clip(1 - PCTPELL_i/0.75,0,1)), 0.05, 0.9) — public control (state funding path), scale, and a fiscal-headroom proxy (public plus low tuition-dependence). (h) ROI: ROI_i = total_pp_i / (G_i*(1-overhead_i)/1e6) = percentage points of expected composite outcome gain per $1M of deployable grant, where overhead_i = 0.12 (Tier 1, >=$3M) or 0.15 (Tier 2) from the 10-20% admin band (exchanges 1,8). ALLOCATION. Rank all eligible schools by rank_score = total_pp_i (at a reference $3M grant) * (0.6 + 0.4*(1 - RET_FT4_i)) — total expected gain tilted by need. Tier 1 = top N_TIER1=12, each grant = clip(0.8*K_SCALE*5*C_PROG*UGDS_i, $4M, $10M) (concentrated, sized to capacity). Tier 2 = next schools at $1.5M each (capped by the scale rule) until the $100M budget is exhausted; the remainder of the budget is unspent rather than diluted below the detectability floor. The funded portfolio (46 schools, $98.2M) plus the next ranked schools form the 1-to-100 prioritized candidate list. DETECTABILITY FLOOR: any school whose in-window composite gain is < FLOOR_PP=1.0 pp is flagged low-confidence (a gain indistinguishable from year-to-year noise, exchange 3); none of the 46 funded schools is below the floor. CALIBRATED PARAMETER TABLE (one line per empirical parameter; values from the 10 expert exchanges, which are the model's empirical source). C_PROG = 1000 $/student/yr, interval [500,1500], source: exchange 6. K_SCALE = 0.5, interval [0.3,0.7], source: exchange 2. T_RAMP4 = 4 yr, interval [3,5], source: exchange 3. T_RAMP2 = 3 yr, interval [2,3], source: exchange 3. P_ABSORB = 0.5, interval [0.5,0.7], source: exchange 4. P_FADE = 0.1, interval [0.0,0.1], source: exchange 4. DELTA0 = 3.0 pp, interval [2,5], source: exchange 7. DELTA_MAX = 8.0 pp, interval [5,10], source: exchange 7. W_RET/W_COMP = 0.6/0.4, source: exchange 10. OVERHEAD1/OVERHEAD2 = 0.12/0.15, interval [0.10,0.20], source: exchanges 1,8. N_TIER1 = 12 (portfolio ~46), interval [8,15], source: exchange 9. FLOOR_PP = 1.0 pp, source: exchange 3. Personnel share 50-70% and grant spend-order, source: exchange 1 (used qualitatively to set the program-cost design). The only numbers in the model not in this table come from the task's own dataset (UGDS, PCTPELL, RET_FT4, completion, CONTROL, net price, PCIP mix).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: RESULTS. The strategy funds 46 schools for $98.2M of the $100M: Tier 1 = 12 concentrated grants averaging ~$4.0M (range $4.0M, sized to capacity), Tier 2 = 34 awards of ~$1.5M (some scale-capped down to $1.28M). It funds ~16,267 students over 5 years, at a mean served share of 0.36 of each school's enrollment. Mean in-window composite gain = 2.29 pp (min 1.89, all above the 1.0 pp detectability floor); mean total expected gain (in-window + post-grant tail) = 3.02 pp per school, 138.7 pp across the portfolio; mean ROI = 2.13 pp per $1M deployable (range 0.99-3.10). The portfolio is heavily 2-year (43/46) and public (45/46), mean enrollment 1,071, mean Pell share 0.641 vs 0.412 universe-wide, mean retention 0.461 vs 0.682 universe-wide — i.e., it tilts to high-need, smaller, public 2-year institutions. Top of the prioritized list (by total expected gain at their tier grant): Arkansas State University-Mountain Home (AR, 1,166, $4.0M, 3.57 pp), Denmark Technical College (SC, 1,804, 3.49), Bladen Community College (NC, 1,016, 3.42), Eastern Idaho Technical College (ID, 575, 3.41), Belmont College (OH, 1,179, 3.41), Tillamook Bay Community College (OR, 514, 3.38), University of Arkansas CC-Batesville (AR, 1,090, 3.36). State spread: NC 10, AR 6, OR 5, SC 4, AL 4. The 1-to-100 candidate list (results/candidate_list.csv) gives the ranked prioritization with per-school grant, funded students, served share, gain, and ROI for the CFO to draw from. TIME DURATION: 5 years, consistent with the funder's plan; the effect ramps to full by year 4 (4-yr) / year 3 (2-yr), with the retention signal earliest and the completion confirmation landing in years 3-5 inside the window. ROI CONCEPT FOR THE CFO (the letter's core): define charitable ROI as expected percentage points of student-outcome gain per dollar of deployable grant, computed on a composite that weights the near-term, independently verifiable retention/persistence measure (0.6) over lagged completion (0.4), with a post-grant persistence discount reflecting whether the school can absorb the program's recurring cost. This is the metric a foundation can actually verify in the field, it is realizable inside the 5-year window, and it rewards the schools whose small, capable, high-need 2-year profile produces the largest measurable gain per dollar. LIMITATIONS AND BIASES. (1) No fiscal data in the 2015 Scorecard (no endowment, surplus, or operating margin), so the absorption probability q is a proxy from control/scale/Pell, not a balance-sheet measure — the single largest source of error, and it biases the model away from exactly the thin-margin private small colleges the expert said are least likely to sustain a program (the model errs on the safe side). (2) The 2015 Scorecard is a snapshot ~11 years before the 2026 run; retention/completion are the most recent cohorts available, so the need and baseline readings may be stale. (3) Effect sizes (DELTA0, persistence, cost) are expert-elicited order-of-magnitude ranges, not school-level causal estimates; the sensitivity sweep shows total portfolio gain is roughly proportional to DELTA0 (2 pp -> 92.5 pp total; 5 pp -> 231.2 pp) and modestly sensitive to C_PROG (500 -> 145.7 pp; 1500 -> 129.8 pp) and K_SCALE (0.3 -> 128.4; 0.7 -> 143.5 pp), so the ranking is stable but the absolute gain scales with the effect-size assumption. (4) Privacy suppression removes debt/repayment variables for small schools, but we do not use debt or earnings as primary outcomes, so this is a minor loss. (5) The model does not model the counterfactual that the same student would have succeeded anyway; the gain is an incremental program effect, so reported pp are upper-bound if the baseline is already on an upward trend. (6) 42 candidate schools had no Scorecard row and were excluded from the list. BIAS: the served-share and need multipliers favor smaller, higher-Pell schools, which is defensible (effects are largest per dollar at that profile) but means the absolute number of students served per school is modest; the concentration tier mitigates by giving the 12 strongest schools enough to serve ~50% of their enrollment.
